beads.title: Match ACL rules whose source is a capability, not just a prefix
beads.description: Upstream lets a tailnet policy name a rule's source by node capability instead of by IP prefix, and this repository decodes that form, compiles it, and can never match it. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, wgengine/filter/filtertype/filtertype.go carries Match.SrcCaps beside Match.Srcs: 'SrcCaps is an alternative way to match packets. If the peer's source IP has one of these capabilities, it's also permitted. The peers are only looked up by their self address (Node.Addresses) and not by subnet routes they advertise.' Control sends such a source as the string cap:<name> in tailcfg.FilterRule; MatchesFromFilterRules splits it into SrcCaps; and wgengine/filter/filter.go threads a CapTestFunc (f.srcIPHasCap) into every matches4.match / matches6.match / matchIPsOnly call in runIn4 and runIn6, so a packet whose source peer holds the named capability is accepted even though no Srcs prefix covers it. The test function is LocalBackend.srcIPHasCapForFilter in ipn/ipnlocal/local.go, and it carries a refusal that must travel with the port: 'return !n.UnsignedPeerAPIOnly() && n.HasCap(cap)' -- an unsigned peer is denied every capability -- plus an explicit guard that the empty capability name matches nothing. Upstream dates this: capability version 100 (2024-06-18) is initial support, capability version 109 (2024-11-18) is 'Client supports filtertype.Match.SrcCaps'. This node declares 125, so control is entitled to compile a cap:-sourced rule for it and to expect it honoured. Every layer here is already right except the last one. ts_packetfilter_serde's SrcIp parses the cap: form into SrcIp::NodeCap (its own doc says 'the type name is a misnomer: the source may not be an IP at all'); ts_packetfilter's rule match tests a rule's capability sources against a supplied set; and the Filter trait threads a CapIter through match_for / matches / can_access from top to bottom. Then both call sites hand it nothing. ts_dataplane::inbound_filter_verdict (ts_dataplane/src/lib.rs) reads '// TODO(npry): wire in nodecaps' and then 'let caps = [];', and ts_runtime::peerapi_doh::dns_source_allowed -- the ACL arm of the peerAPI DNS gate -- does the same and documents it in place. So this node drops a packet a Go client accepts, and answers 403 to a peerAPI DNS query a Go client resolves, on any tailnet whose policy grants access by capability rather than by prefix. It fails closed, which is why it has cost nothing visible; it is still a divergence a control plane can trigger at will. The work is the capability test itself: resolve the source address to a peer (PeerTracker::peer_by_tailnet_ip, which the DoH gate already calls) and pass that peer's node capabilities into can_access at both sites. Both sites must move together, or the dataplane admits a packet the DoH gate refuses from the same peer under the same policy. The cases to pin are the ones that keep it from widening the ACL: a source that resolves to no peer supplies no capabilities and is still judged on prefixes alone; an UnsignedPeerAPIOnly peer supplies none either, per Go's own line; the empty capability name matches nothing; and a rule carrying both Srcs and SrcCaps still accepts on the prefix when the capability is absent. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Apply the shields-up filter to a jailed peer instead of the ordinary ACL
beads.description: Control marks a peer IsJailed when that peer must not be allowed to initiate connections to this node -- upstream's canonical case is a Mullvad-style exit node, a peer this node dials out through and which has no business dialling back in. This repository decodes the flag and ignores it. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, upstream implements it as a second, separate packet filter. ipn/ipnlocal/local.go's updateFilterLocked builds it unconditionally on every netmap -- 'The filter for a jailed node is the exact same as a ShieldsUp filter' -- as filter.NewShieldsUpFilter(localNets, logNets, oldJailedFilter, b.logf), a filter with no rules at all that shares flow state with its predecessor, and installs it with e.SetJailedFilter. net/tstun/wrap.go then chooses between the two per packet: filterPacketInboundFromWireGuard uses the jailed filter when pc.inboundPacketIsJailed(p), and filterPacketOutboundToWireGuard uses it when pc.outboundPacketIsJailed(p), both reading PeerRoute.Jailed out of the route table published by net/routemanager. Because a shields-up filter has no rules, nothing a jailed peer initiates is admitted -- while the reply-admission carve-outs (TCP non-SYN, ICMP responses, the UDP/SCTP reverse-flow cache) still run against the jailed filter's own state, so a connection this node opened to that peer keeps working in both directions. That is the whole point: one-way, not no-way. Capability version 81 (2024-05-06) declares that the client understands Node.IsJailed, and this node declares 125. Here, is_jailed is decoded and dropped: ts_control_serde::Node::is_jailed exists with Go's own doc comment on it, the string appears nowhere else in the tree, ts_control::Node does not carry it, and ts_dataplane::filter_inbound_from_peer takes exactly one filter for every peer in the batch. So a jailed exit node can open a TCP connection to any port this node's ACL happens to leave open -- which, for a node that has selected that peer as its exit node, is precisely the peer with the most reach and the least reason to have it. The mechanism is already present, which is what makes the port tractable: ts_packetfilter's ShieldsUpFilter, wrapped in ts_runtime::packetfilter, is this fork's NewShieldsUpFilter, built today from the local Env::block_incoming knob rather than per peer. The work is to carry is_jailed onto ts_control::Node, build the second filter alongside the first, and select between them per source peer the way Go selects per packet. The negative cases are what make it safe and must be asserted: a reply to a flow this node opened to the jailed peer is still admitted (or selecting a jailed exit node breaks the exit node), an unjailed peer is unaffected, and a peer that becomes unjailed in a later netmap stops being filtered -- the flag is per netmap, not sticky. Read it alongside the TSMP reject path, which already distinguishes a shields-up deny from an ACL deny: a jailed peer's refusal should carry the same reason a Go node's does. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Apply the per-peer masquerade addresses control configures, or stop declaring them
beads.description: When two tailnets are shared, control can tell this node 'peer P knows you as address M' by setting SelfNodeV4MasqAddrForThisPeer (or the v6 field) on P in our netmap. This repository models both fields on the wire and applies neither. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, net/tstun/wrap.go honours them as symmetric NAT in the data plane. peerConfigTable.selectSrcIP rewrites the source of a packet this node originates to M when the destination falls in P's prefix, and refuses to do so when the source is not this node's own native address ('If this packet doesn't originate from this Tailscale node, don't SNAT it (e.g. if we're a subnet router)'). peerConfigTable.mapDstIP rewrites the destination of a packet from P back from M to the native address. Both run through checksum.UpdateSrcAddr / UpdateDstAddr and are documented as never mutating packet length or address family. L7 follows the same rule: ipn/ipnlocal/peerapi.go's isAddressValid accepts a Host header naming M -- and that function is the only part of this upstream touched in the interval, by commit 5186c3f41, which fixed it to require a masquerade match only for the address family the masquerade applies to, because a v6-only masquerade pair still leaves the peer dialling the native v4 peerAPI URL and every fresh connection was getting a 403. Nothing here applies any of it. ts_control_serde::Node models self_node_v4_masq_addr_for_this_peer and its v6 sibling with Go's own comment; neither reaches ts_control::Node; and there is no SNAT or DNAT anywhere in ts_dataplane -- process_outbound runs the capture tee, the host-injected-TSMP drop, the flow-state record and the routing, and never touches an address. ts_runtime::peerapi's is_self_address records the consequence honestly and draws the wrong conclusion from it: its doc says masquerade 'is not implemented at all and there is no current divergence'. The divergence is real, because the behaviour is control-driven and peer-side. Capability versions 64 (2023-03-16) and 87 (2024-08-03, 'SelfNodeV6MasqAddrForThisPeer now works') both sit below the 125 this node declares, so control may configure a masquerade on the strength of that declaration alone. When it does, the peer sends to M, this node receives a packet addressed to an IP it does not own and the netstack drops it; it replies from its native address, which is outside the peer's allowed IPs for it, and the peer drops that. The node is simply unreachable from that peer, with nothing in either log naming a cause. There are two ways to close this and the choice is the bead's real content. Implement it: carry both fields onto ts_control::Node, add the two rewrites to ts_dataplane's inbound and outbound paths with incremental checksum updates, and teach is_self_address the masquerade address per family -- Go's shape after 5186c3f41, not before, since the pre-fix shape 403s a mixed-family peer. Or refuse it by holding the declared capability version below 64, which this tree cannot do, because the declared version already has a floor of 121 for the peer-relay client half. That leaves implementing it, or accepting a knowingly false declaration. Test the refusals with the port: a subnet-routed packet is not SNATed (Go returns early when the source is not the native address), a family with no masquerade configured is untouched, and the checksum is updated incrementally rather than recomputed. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Answer a TSMP ping with a pong, so a Go peer's tailscale ping succeeds
beads.description: A Go peer can send this node a TSMP ping and expects a pong; this node answers nothing, and the peer waits out its timeout while the node sits there working perfectly. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, net/tstun/wrap.go answers it in the wrapper, ahead of any filtering: filterPacketInboundFromWireGuard matches p.AsTSMPPing(), notes activity, calls injectOutboundPong, and returns filter.DropSilently so the ping never reaches the local stack. injectOutboundPong builds a packet.TSMPPongReply carrying the request's 8 bytes of opaque data and this node's peerAPI port (from t.PeerAPIPort), reverses the IP header with ToResponse, and injects it outbound; a header that is neither IPv4 nor IPv6 returns without sending. The other direction is symmetric: an arriving pong goes to OnTSMPPongReceived, which wgengine/userspace.go dispatches through a pongCallback map keyed on those same 8 bytes, and that is how tailscale ping reports an end-to-end round trip a disco ping cannot measure -- a disco ping proves a path, a TSMP ping proves the node is alive and processing packets. This repository names the two type bytes and stops: ts_packet/src/tsmp.rs's TSMP_TYPE_PING and TSMP_TYPE_PONG each carry the doc comment 'Not parsed here'. ts_dataplane's inbound TSMP arm consumes the disco advertisement and the rejected-connection header and lets every other TSMP body through to the ACL step, which accepts it and hands it to the smoltcp netstack, which has no handler for IP protocol 99. It is the same class of silence the TSMP reject work removed from the ACL-drop path, one message type over, and it is peer-observable without any help from control. The send half is the part worth doing first and it is small: ts_packet::tsmp already marshals two TSMP bodies against Go's own layout, so a third is the same shape, and ts_dataplane already has a route for injecting a TSMP message back to a peer (InboundHarvest::rejects_to_send, built for the reject). Fill the pong's PeerAPIPort from the same RejectConfig::peerapi_port the reject path already carries -- that field is exactly Go's t.PeerAPIPort and it is already plumbed. The receive half (matching an inbound pong against an outstanding request) needs a caller here to be worth anything, since Device has no ping surface today, so it can be a separate decision; say which way you went and why. Bring the refusals with it: a body too short to be a ping is not a ping (Go's AsTSMPPing length check), the ping is dropped rather than delivered even when a pong could not be built, and no pong is generated for a header that is neither IPv4 nor IPv6. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Decide the peerAPI's packet-level carve-out, now that both L7 gates exist
beads.description: Upstream pairs a deliberate hole in the packet filter with an access check inside each peerAPI handler; this repository now has the second half and not the first, and the resulting behaviour reads as an oversight. At commit 023255e8a27ec9f6a21d24e3eda21c052ff72af3, net/tstun/wrap.go flips an ACL-refused inbound packet back to Accept when it is a TCP SYN whose destination port is this node's peerAPI port: 'Let peerapi through the filter; its ACLs are handled at L7, not at the packet level.' Every peerAPI handler that needs an access decision then makes it itself -- Taildrop against the file-sharing capability, the DNS proxy against isPeerAPIDNSAllowed in ipn/ipnlocal/peerapi.go. The two are one design, and upstream's reason for it is that a tailnet ACL is written about ports and services, not about the daemon's own peerAPI port, so requiring the ACL to name that port would make Taildrop depend on a rule nobody writes. This tree has the L7 half and not the packet half. The peerAPI DNS source gate landed in ts_runtime/src/peerapi_doh.rs, and ts_runtime/src/peerapi.rs's gate_taildrop is the file-sharing check; but ts_dataplane admits a peerAPI SYN only if some ordinary rule covers it. ts_dataplane's tsmp_reject_for_drop documents the seam exactly -- it suppresses the TSMP reject for a peerAPI-port SYN 'by suppressing the message here rather than by admitting the packet' -- so a peer whose ACL does not cover this node's peerAPI port is dropped and told nothing, where Go would have admitted it and then made an L7 decision. The decision is genuine and should be made deliberately rather than by omission. Adding the carve-out is parity, and it is what makes Taildrop from a Go peer work under an ordinary ACL; it also widens what reaches the peerAPI to every peer, which is safe only because the L7 gates are now in place -- and they were not, before the DNS gate landed. Leaving it out is stricter, and the fork has been running that way; the cost is that Taildrop to this node silently fails on a tailnet where it works for every Go client, and the failure looks like a network problem rather than a policy one. The recommended reading is to add it now that both L7 gates exist, gated exactly as Go gates it -- TCP, SYN only, destination port equal to the peerAPI port, and only when a peerAPI is actually running -- so the hole is no wider than upstream's, with the negative cases asserted: a non-SYN, a UDP datagram, and a SYN to any other port are all still subject to the ACL, and no carve-out applies when no peerAPI is configured. Whichever way it goes, the decision belongs in the code as a comment, because the current state reads as an oversight and is not. See PORTING.md section B.
